title: Testing the Teachers We Follow
english: Logos 3. “My people, your collectors glean you bare, and those who demand payment rule over you” (Isaiah 3:12).

Having declared beforehand, very plainly and quite clearly, that the land of the Jews would suffer the loss of every good thing, and having set out what will happen to those who behaved outrageously toward Christ, he again tries to persuade them in advance to keep away from their offences. With gentle words he all but charms them, to their profit, moving them toward what is better and teaching them to reject those who had become the cause of all their evils.

For I do not think one ought to be fond of submitting to those whose lot is to lead, if they attempt to teach nothing of what serves for profit; nor indeed … worthy of censure what may justly be believed to belong among wicked things. For the excellence of a teacher lies in being able to bring those in his charge to an exact knowledge of what is profitable, to expose as counterfeit whatever by nature does harm, and to bid them refuse what usually does wrong.

And those who are counted among disciples would deserve every praise if they looked not simply at the reputations of their teachers but at the nature of the matters themselves; if they admired their teachers, provided these are upright and knowledgeable and guides to what is best, and found fault with those whose aim is not of this kind.

Some men pasture flocks of sheep on mountains and in glens. But if a pit lies beside the flock, or a mountain precipice, the sheep walk around it and do not throw themselves down to their death; for they are taught, as by an inborn law, that they must spare their own life. Is it not absurd, then, that this should plainly prevail among irrational animals, while in us, though we are rational, there is no knowledge of what is useful and necessary for life?

So even if some of those appointed as our teachers and guides should choose to lead us toward what is not fitting, we must not simply be content to bear with it, nor follow without examination wherever they please; rather, we must test each thing that is to be done … to go toward whatever most often does good.

Now the leaders of the Jews, that is, the scribes and the Pharisees, were clever at collecting gains of money and gathering in the people’s offerings: first fruits, tithes, and all that the Law, as a portion for those whose lot was to serve as priests …
